A.title: Turn the Key Stage 3 rule into an inspected, funded promise
A.answer: The Department for Education has told schools not to start GCSE courses early for large groups or routinely narrow options, but gives no cost, start date or check (s1). Change it: the department adds a ring-fenced grant, so no school pays by cutting subjects or staff, which school leaders warn is the risk without investment (s3). The school inspectorate then checks, in every secondary inspection, how many pupils start GCSEs before Year 10 and whether options narrowed. Each school publishes its Year 7 to 9 timetable and absence rate in plain words. It worked if early starts fall and Year 7 to 9 persistent absence, one in four by Year 9 (s1), stops rising.

B.title: Let each school's local panel decide what Years 7 to 9 are for
B.answer: Instead of the Department for Education setting one rule from the centre (s1), each secondary school's governing body adds a panel drawn by lot from its teachers, parents and Year 7 to 9 pupils. The panel signs off a published three-year plan, including whether any GCSE teaching starts early. That moves the choice away from exam pressure, which 57% of surveyed teachers named a leading influence (s2). The department funds the panels' time, as school leaders warn extra duties without investment risk diluting provision (s3). It worked if absence, which the department says reaches one in four children by Year 9 (s1), falls, and more than 36% of pupils see learning's link beyond exams (s2).
